strengths: The paper addresses a relevant user-level provenance problem through a modular approach compatible with existing bitstring watermarking systems.

Experiments cover three image generators, up to one million simulated users, and several common distortions. Reporting worst-user performance is valuable, and Figure 7 shows improved attribution from A-BSTA over Random and NRG.

The attribution bound provides an interpretable relationship between watermark separation and decoding accuracy. Algorithm pseudocode, selection-time measurements, and explicit acknowledgment of white-box vulnerability are useful.
weaknesses: The false-detection guarantee is not established for the proposed method. Theorem 3 assumes independently selected watermarks, but A-BSTA deliberately selects them dependently; nevertheless, Section 7.6 applies this theorem. Appendix A.4 also factors matching events without establishing their independence for a fixed database. For example, with W={00,11}, uniformly random decoded bits, and threshold 0.75, the actual FDR is 1/2, exceeding the formula's 7/16. Guarantees averaged over random codebooks must be distinguished from guarantees for the deployed codebook.

The binomial analysis relies on unvalidated assumptions. Definitions 3–4 require independent decoded bits, identical per-bit correctness probabilities for watermarked content, and bounds on every bit's bias for unwatermarked content. Estimating average accuracy and aggregate bit frequencies does not establish these conditions. Figure 8's agreement in average performance does not validate the tail probabilities or robustness guarantees.

Novelty and baseline coverage are insufficiently established. Assigning user codewords and applying nearest-codeword decoding closely relates to classical fingerprinting and error-correcting codes, yet these connections receive inadequate treatment. A-BSTA mainly introduces random initialization and truncated search into an existing algorithm. Comparisons against structured codes and computationally matched random-search methods are needed to establish its value.

The evidence for low false-detection rates and very large deployments is inadequate. Only 1,000 negative images are evaluated; even zero observed errors permits an approximately 0.3% one-sided 95% upper confidence bound. The 100-million-user result assumes decoding accuracy and codeword separation without demonstrating them at that scale. Table 4's 6% FDR upper bound does not establish the introduction's near-zero-FDR claim.

Robustness evaluation is limited to one modified HiDDeN implementation at 128×128 resolution, corruption families included during training, and one black-box attack. This supports performance in those settings but leaves broader robustness insufficiently tested. The reported SSIM measures post-processing damage, while the perceptual cost of embedding the watermark itself is not adequately evaluated.

The text experiment uses human-written WikiText-2 segments rather than generated LLM outputs. It also substantially increases the watermark loss weight and constrains paraphrase length, without reporting fluency or semantic preservation. Consequently, attribution accuracy alone does not establish a useful watermarking solution for AI-generated text.

Practical scalability and reproducibility remain incomplete. Attribution scans the watermark database, but inference latency, throughput, and memory scaling are not reported. The 24 ms average watermark-selection time does not resolve these deployment costs, and implementation availability, hardware details, and uncertainty across training or codebook seeds are insufficiently documented.
